h1: What is actually inside a seaweed extract, and what should a buyer ask?
title: What's inside a seaweed extract? A buyer's guide | GBO
desc: Alginates, laminarin, fucoidan, mannitol, betaines and growth signals: what they are, how they vary, and what a label cannot tell a buyer.
answer: A seaweed extract is a mixture, not one ingredient. Brown seaweeds carry alginates, laminarin, fucoidan and mannitol. Red seaweeds carry carrageenans. Betaines and growth-signal compounds appear too. The mix shifts with species, season and extraction, so buyers should ask for batch data on named compounds and how each was measured.
sections: the-compounds-to-ask-about
The compounds worth asking about

This is a buying guide. It does not cover how these compounds act in the plant. It covers what they are, and what you can fairly ask a supplier to show.

CompoundWhat it isWhat reviews reportWhat to ask
AlginatesCell-wall polysaccharide of brown seaweeds17 to 45% of brown seaweed. The balance of its M and G units varies with species and harvest period.How much is in this liquid, and on what basis?
LaminarinStorage polysaccharide of brown seaweeds, about 20 to 25 units longFucoidan and laminarin together: 5 to 20% of brown seaweed.Was it measured on its own, or folded into total carbohydrate?
FucoidanSulfated polysaccharide containing fucoseReported sizes run from about 40 kDa to 1,600 kDa.Which method measured it? Is there any size data?
MannitolA polyol, described as an osmoprotectant7.5% quoted for Ascophyllum nodosum. It changes through the growth cycle in Indian Sargassum (see below).Which harvest period does this batch come from?
BetainesGlycine betaine and related compounds, widespread in marine algaeReported in an Ascophyllum extract and in Kappaphycus alvarezii.Which betaine, how much, and by which method?
Growth-signal compoundsCytokinins, auxins, gibberellins and similarPresent in small quantities. Published auxin figures disagree widely.What was the method? Was it this batch?
CarrageenansSulfated polysaccharide of red seaweed cell wallsKappa-carrageenan is the major cell-wall component of Kappaphycus alvarezii.Does it stay in the liquid or leave with the solids?

Most percentages above describe the seaweed itself, or leave the basis unstated. They do not describe what is in your drum.
species-sets-the-list
Species sets the starting list

The first split is brown against red. Alginates, fucoidan and laminarin are named as brown seaweed polysaccharides. Red seaweeds carry carrageenans instead. So a red seaweed product sold on its alginate content needs an explanation.

Inside the brown group, figures also move. For alginates alone, reviews give 17 to 45% of brown seaweeds, 10 to 40% of dry weight, and 15 to 30% by dry weight for Ascophyllum. One review lists Ascophyllum at 28% alginic acid, 11.6% fucoidans, 7.5% mannitol and 4.5% laminarin, without stating the basis. Another lists fucoidans for Sargassum wightii.

Red seaweed varies too. A review of Kappaphycus notes composition differences between strains, cultivation depths and stress conditions. For a side-by-side of the three seaweeds used most, see our species comparison.
season-and-process
Season and process change the same species

Harvest timing matters. A study of Sargassum wightii and Turbinaria conoides from the Gulf of Mannar found mannitol highest early in the growth cycle, from May to August, and lowest after reproductive structures appeared. Alginic acid yield was high during peak growth and fruiting. Reviews also report considerable seasonal variation in Ascophyllum meal. One review of algal biostimulants says that harvesting in different seasons and years hinders tight technical standards and constant quality.

Process matters as much. The common industrial route for Ascophyllum is NaOH or KOH at 70 to 100°C. It breaks polysaccharides into smaller oligomers and creates compounds not present in the raw seaweed. Under high-pressure alkaline extraction, some hormonal molecules can be degraded. Breakdown is not automatically bad: the same review calls the resulting oligomers highly bioactive. The point is that the bottle no longer matches the seaweed.

One study compared two Ascophyllum extracts directly. Their compositions differed significantly, with a 4-fold gap in polyphenols. Applied to the model plant Arabidopsis, one changed the activity of 4.47% of the transcriptome and the other 0.87%. That is a laboratory gene-expression result, not a promise for any product. It does show that one species name can cover two different materials.
growth-signal-numbers
Why a growth-signal number needs a method beside it

Be most careful here. A review of Ascophyllum products records about 50 mg of auxin per gram of dry extract from earlier reports, and 25 to 35 ng per gram from a later study using liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry. That is a gap of more than a million-fold. The authors link such variation to extraction, processing, origin and season.

Method can move the answer too. A review of Kappaphycus describes one comparison of three methods on sap, and says the ESI-MS values were more reliable, because impurities interfered less. So a hormone figure with no method beside it cannot be compared with anything. A figure taken from a paper says nothing about your batch.
what-a-label-cannot-tell-you
What a label cannot tell you

In India, seaweed extracts fall under category (a) of Schedule VI, botanical extracts. Grade names such as those on our Schedule VI page give species, extract percentage and form. Confirm the current specification for a grade in the latest Gazette, and check with your state agriculture department.

Species, percentage and form are useful. On their own, they do not tell you:

  • How much alginate, laminarin, fucoidan, mannitol or betaine is present.
  • Whether two products at the same percentage hold the same mix.
  • When and where the seaweed was harvested.
  • Whether the process was alkaline, acidic, heated or mild.
  • How the product will perform on a given crop.

Do not swing to the other extreme and rank products on one compound. In a study of extracts from Laminaria and Ascophyllum given to maize for two days, the authors found chemical features appeared crucial in predicting response. Yet two extracts that varied greatly in composition produced similar positive effects. Composition data narrows the choice. A fair trial still has to finish it.
what-to-request
What to request from a supplier

These requests go beyond the standard label and documents checklist. They are specific to composition.

  • Species. The botanical name, and the ratio for any blend.
  • Origin. Harvest region and period, or whether the seaweed is farmed.
  • Process. The extraction type, in plain terms.
  • Basis. Whether each percentage refers to dry seaweed, dry extract or the liquid as sold.
  • Method. The test method for every named compound.
  • Batch. Results from the batch on offer, plus earlier batches to show the spread.
  • Source of the figure. Measured on this product, or quoted from literature.

A supplier may not have all of this. An honest "we do not measure that" tells you more than a textbook table on a data sheet.
what-gbo-can-say
What we can say from our own plant

Gujarat Bio Organics has worked with farmers since 2006 and runs its own plant at GIDC Shihor, Bhavnagar, with monthly capacity of 100 KL liquid and 2,500 t solid. We hold Gujarat NOCs for 36 FCO Schedule VI biostimulant grades and 11 biofertiliser types. Our seaweed and humic extraction is mild and in-house, without harsh chemicals, very high pH or heat.

That matters for this topic in one way. Process is the variable a trader often cannot explain, and for our in-house extraction it is known. A mild process should not be expected to give the same mix as a hot alkaline one, and we do not claim one mix is right for every crop. Our seaweed grades include Ascophyllum nodosum, Kappaphycus alvarezii and Sargassum tenerrimum.
faq: Does a higher seaweed extract percentage mean more alginate or laminarin?
Not necessarily. The percentage does not say which compounds make it up. Ask for measured values, and ask whether each refers to dry seaweed, dry extract or the liquid as sold.
Do red seaweed extracts contain alginates?

Reviews name alginates, fucoidan and laminarin as brown seaweed polysaccharides, and carrageenans as the red seaweed group. If a red seaweed product is sold on alginate content, ask for the test report and method.
Can I compare cytokinin or auxin figures between two suppliers?

Only if the method and the basis match and both were measured on the batch offered. Published auxin figures for one seaweed differ by more than a million-fold, and reviews link this to extraction, processing, origin and season.

It is not simply good or bad. It is widely used and it changes the material: polysaccharides break into smaller oligomers, new compounds form and some hormone molecules can degrade. The practical step is to know which process was used.
Does Schedule VI listing tell me the compound content?

A grade name gives species, extract percentage and form. For the compound data discussed here, ask the supplier. Confirm the current grade specification in the latest Gazette and check with your state agriculture department.
